gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2's solar input (12–60 V, 20 A max) only accepts the two 200 W panels of its 400 W kit wired in series. In series the panels give 2 × 24.6 V = 49.2 V open-circuit. In parallel they would push 2 × 10.8 A = 21.6 A into a 20 A input. A third panel cannot be added either way: three in series give 73.8 V, which is over 60 V. The 2 × 350 W kit cannot run in series at all, because 2 × 33 V = 66 V is over 60 V.
standout_why: Victron's cited guide explains Voc in general and that a controller's first number is its maximum PV voltage (the 100/30 example). It never checks a panel string against a power station's input, never mentions an input-current cap that clips parallel panels, and never mentions power stations at all. The Renogy page ChatGPT cited returned only navigation to WebFetch (6,865 characters, no article body), so I could not compare it. smartrvhub.com, the #4 result dated 2026-11-11, has no Voc or input-limit discussion and no power stations. powerinverters.com's kit guide has no Voc, current-cap or series/parallel guidance. I could not open tucsonrvsolar.com because of a certificate error. This finding settles how the kit is wired and which BLUETTI bundle to pick (2 × 200 W rather than 2 × 350 W). It also rules out ChatGPT's '600 W' suggestion on this station with these panels. I scored it 2 rather than 3 because Victron already covers the general idea of a maximum PV voltage.
kit_items: Power station (battery + MPPT + inverter): BLUETTI Elite 200 V2. StorageReview measured 1.91 kWh delivered. Against Victron's 720 Wh/day RV example that is about 2.6 days with no sun. Its rated 2,600 W AC output and 12 V/10 A car outlet cover a 12 V compressor fridge, which smartrvhub lists at 40–80 W.

Solar: 2 × BLUETTI SP200L 200 W, wired in series. That gives 49.2 V Voc, under the 60 V limit, and 10.8 A Isc, under the 20 A limit. 400 W of panels is just under Victron's recommended 450–500 W for 720 Wh/day.
Cable: BLUETTI 20 A MC4 to XT60 solar charging cable, if the bundle doesn't include one. Its 20 A rating matches the Elite 200 V2's 20 A input.

findings.label: Solar input window
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh
findings.note: Maker's US page. StorageReview repeats the same figures: '12V to 60V, 20A max', up to 1,000 W.

findings.label: Open-circuit voltage / short-circuit current
findings.note: Two in series: 2 × 24.6 = 49.2 V, under 60 V, with 10.8 V of headroom; current stays at 10.8 A, under 20 A. Two in parallel: 2 × 10.8 = 21.6 A, over the 20 A input. Three in series: 3 × 24.6 = 73.8 V, over 60 V. So the kit works only as 2S, and a third panel won't fit.

findings.label: Open-circuit voltage
findings.note: Two in series: 2 × 33 = 66 V, over the Elite 200 V2's 60 V. So the Elite 200 V2 + 2 × 350 W bundle ($2,148.00) has to be wired in parallel, and the 20 A input cap then limits what it can deliver.

findings.label: Measured usable energy
findings.value: 1.91 kWh delivered (about 92% of 2,073.6 Wh rated); 2.44 kWh drawn to recharge
findings.source_title: Portable power meets lab-grade reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 review (StorageReview, Dylan Dougherty, 2025-04-25)
findings.note: The test load isn't stated. 1,910 Wh ÷ 720 Wh/day (Victron's example) = 2.65 days with no solar.

findings.label: Example RV daily load and solar sizing
findings.value: 720 Wh/day; 144 W minimum array at 5 peak sun hours; 450–500 W recommended
findings.source_title: How to Size a Solar System for Your RV | Victron Energy
findings.note: Load: laptop 60 W × 3 h = 180 Wh, 12 V 70 L fridge 500 Wh, lights 10 W × 4 h = 40 Wh. Minimum array: 720 ÷ 5 PSH = 144 W. Victron suggests roughly tripling that to refill in 4–5 PSH. This kit at nameplate: 400 W × 5 PSH = 2,000 Wh/day before losses. Empty to full: 2,073.6 Wh ÷ 400 W ≈ 5.2 h of full nameplate sun.
